system.aiNote: Use Case A (Auto Dispatch) is a deterministic weighted-sum ranking with no LLM. Use Cases B (Job Summarisation Copilot) and C (Parts Finder) are AI-assisted: a self-hosted qwen3-vl-moe generation model and bge-m3 embeddings served behind a LiteLLM gateway, with Google Gemini wired as an optional external fallback that ships off by default. C runs retrieval-augmented part prediction over a vector store of historical dispatch reasons.
system.multiSystemNote: Existing AWS-hosted FieldJetX platform (.NET APIs, SQL Server) + new AWS Auto-Dispatch tier (ElastiCache for Redis, ECS Fargate, Amazon SNS) + new Azure AI tier (FastAPI on Container Apps, Cosmos DB Mongo, vector store) + on-prem ClimatePros model hardware (LiteLLM/vLLM), reached across two named cross-cloud/cross-network seams, plus two third-party integrations (Azuga fleet telematics for travel time, United Refrigeration's CP API Gateway for the vendor parts tier).

verdictReason: No unresolved Blockers — the prior review's Gemini/third-party-data contradiction is cleanly closed. The 7.4 average is held down by seven Majors, most of them external-dependency confirmations (Azure list pricing, an existing telematics contract's call-volume coverage, a client DBA sign-off, on-prem hardware access) rather than analytical gaps, plus one concrete compliance-flow omission (the EPA-tracked refrigerant-form hard block) and one undefined data-deletion mechanism.
executiveSummary: This v1.3 is the 'how' companion to the Stream 1 Scope Document, covering deterministic Auto Dispatch (A) plus AI-assisted Job Summarisation (B) and Parts Finder (C), and its own changelog shows it closing a prior round-2 review (one Blocker, 25 Majors) with real engineering depth — fencing-token locking for A's assignment race, a fail-closed PII/pricing scrub with a CI-gating leakage eval, and an eval-gated CI/CD pipeline with per-runtime rollback. Cross-checking against the companion Scope Document confirms nearly all of that prior review's fidelity gaps are now closed (the cross-tier buffer, the Gemini contradiction, the CI/CD gap), but surfaces one this review is the first to flag: the completeness-gate language ('never blocks Save') drops scope B4's one hard exception — a missing, EPA-tracked refrigerant form must block submission. At 7.4/10 with no unresolved Blockers, the score is held down by seven Majors that are mostly external-dependency confirmations the document already tracks as its own Open Items (real Azure pricing, an existing telematics contract's coverage of new call volume, client DBA sign-off, on-prem hardware access) rather than places the architecture failed to think something through — a materially better position than hiding the unknowns, but it means the headline cost total and dispatch-capacity ceiling aren't independently verifiable yet. A team could start building from this today; a short, mostly ClimatePros/vendor-side punch list should close before full production reliance.
strengths: A's assignment correctness under failure is genuinely rigorous: per-technician fencing tokens plus XAUTOCLAIM recovery give a proven, textbook-correct answer to the exact 'stale worker writes after losing its lock' race the prior review flagged as unresolved.

The PII/pricing scrub (§6B/§12) is a fail-closed, provider-agnostic, CI-gated control with a per-call audit field and an honestly stated residual risk — one of the more complete AI data-boundary controls this reviewer has seen described at the architecture stage.

CI/CD & release management (§11) now covers all three runtimes (Container Apps, ECS Fargate, on-prem model-tag pinning) with concrete rollback mechanics and an eval gate that blocks, not just flags, a bad B/C release.
The document's own Changelog and 14-item Open Items appendix map every outstanding decision to a 'why it matters' note — surfaced uncertainty that makes a build team's risk lower, not hidden.

B and C's eval design shows real ML maturity: an engagement-independent quality signal (catching edit-rate improving only because technicians stopped reading) and C's admission criteria explicitly avoid the model reinforcing its own unverified predictions.

areas.name: Overview & Problem Framing
areas.assessment: The problem framing is crisp and consistent with the scope document's three bottlenecks, and the document adds a genuinely useful cover apparatus (document-control table, an explicit 'how to read this' cloud-placement rule, and a 14-item Open Items appendix). B's success target is now correctly aligned with the scope document's own 'up to roughly half' framing (resolving the prior review's numeric mismatch). The residual gap is that A and C's own success measures (scope §9: cascade-completion share, on-time-arrival share, and override rate for A; top-3 hit-rate and sourcing-session resolution rate for C) aren't restated or cross-referenced here — only B's target appears in §1 — and the Table of Contents' page numbers drift increasingly out of sync with the actual document from §4 onward.
areas.suggestions: Add a one-line cross-reference for A's and C's success measures in §1 (even just 'see scope §9') so a reader doesn't need the companion document to know what 'success' means for those two use cases. Regenerate the Table of Contents' page numbers against the final v1.3 pagination.
areas.strengths: The document-control table, explicit reading rules, and Open Items appendix are unusually transparent framing devices; the B target now matches the scope document's own phrasing exactly.

areas.name: Architecture & System Design
areas.assessment: Three diagrams (unified, A-detail, B&C-detail) are clear, mutually consistent, and match the prose; every component has an explicit single responsibility, and the SQL-connection isolation ('workers and the AI server hold no SQL connection') is a clean, auditable boundary. The admission-control design for the AI gateway (a semaphore sized to measured capacity, a bounded queue, fast 429/503+Retry-After, autoscaling triggered by queue-wait rather than raw concurrency) correctly identifies that the model server, not the stateless proxy, is the real bottleneck — a distinction many specs miss. Two smaller gaps remain: the tie-break rule's first criterion ('lowest ETA') doesn't quite match scope A2 Rule 5 ('fewer minutes left on the current job') — these diverge whenever two technicians share an equal ETA via different free-time/travel-time splits — and the candidate-eligibility filter (the workload limit and emergency-stacking rule in scope A2 Rules 1 and 6) is asserted only as 'eligible technicians… read via the .NET APIs' without restating the filter itself.
areas.suggestions: In §6A, replace 'lowest ETA first' with 'fewest minutes left on the current job' as the tie-break's first criterion to match scope A2 Rule 5 exactly (a one-line pseudocode fix). Add a short paragraph confirming whether the workload-limit/emergency-stacking eligibility check (A2 Rules 1 & 6) is existing platform data Auto Dispatch reads, or new logic this project computes — and if new, state the predicate.
areas.strengths: The fencing-token design for A's assignment race, the AWS/Azure/on-prem boundary rules, and the gateway admission-control design are all well above typical spec-stage rigor.

areas.name: Feature Flows & System Sequencing
areas.assessment: This is close to the document's strongest section: full end-to-end flows with diagrams for all three use cases, and an exceptional unhappy-path treatment — offer-timeout cascade and human escalation, worker-crash recovery via XAUTOCLAIM, stale-fence-token rejection, a clean 409 contract for the 'two technicians accept at once' race, vendor-tier-drops-not-request behaviour for C, and model-throttling retry/backoff. The one material gap: scope's B4/§7 states unambiguously (and twice) that the completeness gate has exactly one hard-block exception — a missing refrigerant form, an EPA-tracked record — while everything else stays a soft prompt. This architecture's flow description doesn't carry that exception forward; §12's 'never blocks Save (every failure mode degrades to manual recap)' reads as an unqualified absolute, and nothing in §5's Summarise & Review loop or §6B's normalise-and-submit logic mentions a refrigerant-specific hard stop. A build team following only this document could reasonably implement B's gate as always-soft, missing the one legally-relevant block scope requires.
areas.suggestions: Add one explicit rule to §5B/§6B (and soften §12's 'never blocks Save' with the same carve-out): submission is blocked in exactly one case — refrigerant mentioned in the note but the refrigerant compliance form not completed — matching scope B4 Rule 4 and §7 verbatim. This is deterministic, rule-based logic, consistent with the rest of B's non-AI completeness checks.
areas.strengths: The per-use-case failure-mode tables (§11) and the fencing-token/XAUTOCLAIM recovery design for A are the most thorough unhappy-path treatment in the document; the late-accept 409 contract cleanly closes a real race condition.

areas.name: Data Schema & Modeling
areas.assessment: Structurally strong: Redis structures are fully specified (keys, TTLs, purpose, self-cleaning semantics); the MongoDB collections carry indicative field-level shapes with types, indexes, and a schemaVersion field for forward-only migration; the one SQL schema change A makes is scoped precisely and sequenced expand→migrate→contract. Two real gaps hold this back from 'Good': the vector-store seeding decision is still open, and the document's own math shows the current sizing assumption is stale by roughly two orders of magnitude (200,000+ jobs/6 months vs. a superseded 3-4K estimate still driving §10's cost line) — a real, quantified, unresolved discrepancy, not just a pending confirmation. Separately, no cascading-deletion mechanism is defined for B's MongoDB records (summaries, summary_edits), which the document itself flags as 'original records, not rebuildable' — unlike C's re-derivable vector index, there is currently no way to honour a SQL-side deletion request against these collections.
areas.suggestions: Resolve the §7C seeding decision (filtered subset vs. full corpus, Open Item #3) and re-derive the vector-store sizing, index-tier, and §10 cost line from the real 200,000+/6-month volume rather than the superseded figure. Define the cascading-deletion mechanism for summaries/summary_edits before this becomes a real customer request — even a stated interim answer (e.g., manual DBA-assisted deletion keyed by dispatchId) is better than an open question with no fallback.
areas.strengths: The Redis-structure table (key/purpose/TTL/self-cleaning) is a model of clarity for an ephemeral coordination layer, and the schemaVersion + N/N-1 reader-compatibility rule for Mongo is a genuinely sound forward-migration approach.

areas.name: API Contracts
areas.assessment: A major improvement over the prior draft: a companion OpenAPI 3.1 file (Stream1-AI-API.openapi.yaml v1.0.0) is now explicitly named and versioned, with pydantic models and the .NET typed client generated from it so implementation can't silently drift from the contract. Every endpoint carries a stated caller, purpose, and latency budget; the standard error envelope (machine code, message, correlation requestId, 400/401/403/404/409/500 semantics) is consistent across all three use cases; idempotency is explicitly called out for mutating operations (the completions push, the late-accept 409 contract); and the AI model-call contract now states a hard timeout and a structured-output enforcement mechanism. The residual gaps are narrow: the max-token ceiling is asserted qualitatively without a number, and this review could not verify the referenced OpenAPI file's actual contents since it wasn't provided alongside the architecture document.
areas.suggestions: State the actual max-token ceiling value alongside the ~10s timeout. Confirm the crossTierBufferMinutes MIN-MAX range with ClimatePros so §6C's one open numeric detail closes.
areas.strengths: Contract-first codegen (pydantic + .NET client generated from one OpenAPI file), the shared error envelope, and the late-accept 409 design are a strong, verifiable API baseline for this stage.

areas.name: Libraries, Frameworks & Tech Stack
areas.assessment: Concrete libraries are named for the full async/AI stack (FastAPI, Uvicorn, pydantic, httpx, redis.asyncio, aioboto3, LiteLLM, vLLM), the embedding-model ambiguity the prior review flagged is now fully resolved (bge-m3, 1024-dim, explicitly the sole model, with the earlier nomic-embed references superseded), and LiteLLM's provider-agnostic routing remains a sound lock-in mitigation. Terraform is named as the cross-cloud IaC tool with a clear rationale. What's still asserted rather than shown: the generation model's exact tag/revision, parameter count, and quantisation remain placeholders pending on-prem hardware access, and the claim that self-hosted model/tooling licences are 'confirmed for commercial deployment' isn't backed by a specific licence name or citation anywhere in the document.
areas.suggestions: Once on-prem hardware access lands (Open Item #1), populate the model tag/revision and quantisation scheme. Add a one-line licence citation per self-hosted component rather than an unqualified 'confirmed' claim, and add representative version numbers for the named Python libraries alongside the 'version-pinned in a lockfile' claim.
areas.strengths: The embedding-model identity is now unambiguous and consistently pinned throughout the document — a clean resolution of what was a self-flagged internal contradiction in the prior draft.

areas.name: Observability & Traceability
areas.assessment: The correlation architecture is sound — one OpenTelemetry trace per request across every hop including the cross-cloud spans, with requestId joining traces, logs, and the AI-specific Mongo collections. llm_calls captures the full artifact needed to debug a bad generation (promptScrubbed, completionRaw, tokens, latency, outcome, and a scrubOutcome audit field), and part_predictions captures the complete retrieval intermediate state (neighbours, cosine distances, the threshold gate, accumulated scores and confidence) — exactly what 'strong' looks like for debugging a bad AI decision. The 11-row alert table is unusually comprehensive, covering business-level signals (an AI-assist usage cliff), cost signals (metered geo spend), and AI-specific integrity signals (served-model-tag divergence) alongside standard infra alerts. The one gap: every single alert's Owner column reads 'to assign — techjays on-call / ClimatePros ops', meaning no signal actually has a named accountable party yet.
areas.suggestions: Assign a real owner (team or role, not 'to assign') to each alert-table row before go-live — an 11-signal table with no accountable owner risks nothing actually getting paged when it fires.
areas.strengths: Cross-cloud trace correlation, full prompt/completion capture per model call, and the retrieval-intermediate capture in part_predictions together give this system better AI debuggability than most production deployments this reviewer has seen at this stage.

areas.name: Evaluation Strategy
areas.assessment: This is one of the strongest sections in the document. B's eval loop is genuinely mature: a versioned, CI-gating eval set rebuilt from real corrections; a headline metric (edit-rate/section) paired with a thresholded drift monitor (not just a trend line); adversarial/prompt-injection guardrail cases; a groundedness eval requiring LLM-as-judge to be validated against human labels before it's trusted; a numeric, fails-closed release gate (target/minimum per metric, a 2-percentage-point regression tolerance, a 200-item eval-set floor); and — genuinely sophisticated — an engagement-independent quality signal that catches the specific failure mode where edit-rate falls only because technicians stopped reading drafts, not because the model improved. C now has the dataset, metric (top-3 hit-rate, matching the scope document's own success measure), and trigger (re-run before any embedding/index change, with a regression block) it previously lacked, with a correction-based loop mirroring B's planned as the next phase. The only residual gaps are that the actual numeric gate values (target/minimum) are still placeholders pending the pilot baseline, and C's correction-based loop isn't live yet — both reasonably staged for a pre-launch document.
areas.suggestions: Ratify the release-gate numbers at the pilot baseline (Open Item #14) before go-live, since the release gate fails closed without them. Consider bringing forward at least a minimal version of C's correction-based loop alongside B's rather than deferring it wholesale to Phase 2.
areas.strengths: The Goodhart's-law-aware engagement-independent quality signal and the LLM-as-judge validation requirement show real ML engineering maturity, well beyond what most specs at this stage attempt.

areas.name: Feedback Loops & Continuous Improvement
areas.assessment: Both B and C have explicit, diagrammed self-learning loops (Persist & Learn for B; the indexing/self-learning loop for C), with prompt and model versioning tying production behaviour to a specific, traceable change (ticket_standard.md is versioned; the served model tag is recorded per call and alerted on divergence from the pinned tag). C's index-admission criteria are a genuine standout: completions are excluded or down-weighted when the prediction was accepted without a technician edit, specifically to avoid the self-reinforcing loop of the model learning from its own unverified output — a subtle failure mode most specs never consider. The one shared gap with EVL above: C's correction-based feedback loop (bringing technician accept/reject signal fully into future re-weighting) is still 'planned Phase-2,' so C's flywheel is thinner than B's at launch, even though the pre-launch backtest gate protects quality in the meantime.
areas.suggestions: Same as EVL: consider whether a minimal version of C's correction-based loop can ship alongside B's rather than as a wholesale Phase-2 deferral, since the self-reinforcement safeguard already built (index-admission criteria) suggests the team has already thought through the hard part.
areas.strengths: The self-reinforcement-avoidance design in C's index-admission criteria (down-weighting unedited accepted predictions) is a genuinely sophisticated, rarely-seen safeguard for a retrieval-augmented feedback loop.

areas.name: AI Compliance, Safety & Governance
areas.assessment: The core privacy design is excellent: the PII/pricing scrub is deterministic, code-level, and provider/runtime-agnostic, with a field allow-list as the primary control, pattern-class matching as a secondary control, fail-closed behaviour on any scrub error or timeout, a CI-gated leakage eval asserting zero leaks per entity class, a per-call audit field (scrubOutcome), and — genuinely to its credit — an honestly stated residual risk (a free-text name absent from the structured record can evade value-matching). The prior review's Blocker (Gemini contradicting a 'never sent to a third party' claim) is now cleanly resolved: Gemini ships off by default, is technically unreachable while disabled, and enabling it requires a documented future data-use decision. Two real gaps keep this out of 'Good': first, no cascading-deletion mechanism exists yet for B's non-rebuildable MongoDB records against SQL-side deletion requests (shared with the DAT finding above); second, the Dev environment's entire justification for letting Gemini process data rests on the data being 'de-identified/synthetic' — but the actual de-identification technique (which fields, what method, whether it's the same scrub as production or something else) is not specified anywhere, only the requirement that it happen.
areas.suggestions: Define the cascading-deletion mechanism for summaries/summary_edits (Open Item #10) — even an interim, manual process is better than none. Before Dev is allowed to run against Gemini, specify the actual de-identification/synthesis method (Open Item #13) in enough detail that someone could audit it — 'de-identified' is a claim, not yet a described control.
areas.strengths: The PII/pricing scrub specification (§6B/§12) — fail-closed, provider-agnostic, CI-gated, audited per call, with an honestly stated residual risk — is one of the most complete AI data-boundary controls this reviewer has seen described at the architecture stage.

areas.name: Infrastructure & Environment Setup
areas.assessment: A substantial improvement: three isolated environments with explicit separation (queues, databases, indexes, keys never shared down), Terraform as a single cross-cloud IaC workflow with remote state and locking, secrets resolved from Key Vault/IAM at deploy time only, two named cross-cloud network seams each with a target state and a documented interim fallback with compensating controls, and — a genuine gap-closer from the prior review — an explicit RPO/RTO backup policy per data store. The capacity-validation plan (a Staging load test at projected peak, gating Phase-3 expansion) is a well-designed answer to the scope document's own peak-concurrency requirement. What keeps this at 'Adequate' rather than 'Good': the core serving facts that plan is supposed to validate — exact model tag, GPU/VRAM, measured throughput — are all still placeholders, so the system's real capacity is genuinely unknown today; and the entire '~$0 marginal cost' travel-time design (a load-bearing assumption for both INF and cost) rests on an unconfirmed fact — that ClimatePros' existing Azuga contract actually covers the new ~28,000 lookups/day this feature adds.
areas.suggestions: Prioritise the on-prem integration test and hardware-capacity measurement (Open Item #1) — everything else in §4's capacity story depends on it. Get written confirmation from ClimatePros that the Azuga contract's terms cover the new call volume (Open Item #11) before relying on the ~$0 assumption in any client conversation; if it doesn't, the metered-API fallback (~$4,000-4,200/month) needs to be budgeted instead.
areas.strengths: The RPO/RTO-per-store backup policy, the Terraform-across-both-clouds IaC design, and the two-seam network topology with named target states and compensating controls are a clear, well-reasoned infrastructure story.

areas.name: CI/CD & Release Management
areas.assessment: This is the most-improved section relative to the prior review, and it shows: an automated build-test-lint-vulnerability-scan pipeline; staged Dev→Staging→Prod promotion where a failed eval set actually blocks a B/C release rather than merely flagging it; revision-based rollback for all three runtimes (Container Apps, ECS Fargate, and on-prem model-tag re-pinning), each with a concrete, one-step revert mechanism; and a genuinely thorough migration strategy covering all three stores — SQL's expand→migrate→contract sequencing, MongoDB's versioned forward-only schemaVersion with an N/N-1 reader-compatibility rule, and the vector store's dual-index build-then-swap cutover. Model releases are treated as a first-class deployment concern (pinned tags, a served-tag-divergence alert, and a fully sequenced combined procedure for embedding-model changes: eval gate → parallel index → backtest → swap → retained rollback window). The only residual items are role-assignment placeholders, not structural gaps.
areas.suggestions: Confirm the specific role/party for triggering a model-tag change (currently '<to confirm>') and settle the .NET-side completion-push trigger mechanism (synchronous vs. outbox+scheduled drain) and its owner (Open Item #4) — the document itself correctly notes the outbox option is more robust under AI-tier outages.
areas.strengths: The per-runtime rollback design and the eval-gate-as-release-block for B/C are genuinely exemplary for an architecture-stage document — most specs at this stage don't get this specific about deployment mechanics.

areas.name: Cost Projection
areas.assessment: The structure here is genuinely strong: real, shown cost formulas rather than conjured numbers; a three-scenario sensitivity table (Light/Typical/Heavy); a clear fixed-floor-vs-variable breakdown; and a prominent, hard-to-miss 'Pending re-pricing' warning box that stops a reader from mistaking the totals for a budget figure. The travel-time cost decision is a standout: the document quantifies the rejected alternative (~$4,000-4,200/month for a metered maps API) against the chosen path (~$0, riding an existing contract) — real unit economics driving a real decision. What keeps this at 'Adequate': three separate, unresolved facts each drive a real chunk of the total — the three largest Azure/AI-tier lines still use AWS rate cards, not real Azure prices; the vector-store line (~$5/month) still reflects the superseded, roughly 200x-too-small sizing; and the entire travel-time '~$0' line depends on an unconfirmed Azuga contract-coverage assumption. None of these are hidden — all three are flagged in the document itself — but together they mean the headline ~$179-255/month total isn't yet a number a client could budget against. No per-technician or per-dispatch unit economic is given either.
areas.suggestions: Get real Azure list pricing (Open Item #2) before this table is used in any budget conversation. Re-derive the vector-store cost line once the §7C seeding decision lands. Confirm the Azuga contract's coverage so the travel-time line either stays at ~$0 or is corrected to the ~$4,000/month metered alternative. Add a simple per-technician or per-dispatch unit economic alongside the monthly totals.
areas.strengths: Showing actual cost formulas, a three-scenario sensitivity table, and a quantified build-vs-buy decision for travel time — plus proactively and prominently flagging which numbers are still provisional — is well above the bar for this stage.

findings.finding: Scope B4 Rule 4 and §7 both state, unambiguously, that the completeness gate has exactly one hard-block exception — a missing refrigerant compliance form (an EPA-tracked record) must stop submission, while every other gap is a soft prompt. The architecture's own non-goals language ('never blocks Save — every failure mode degrades to manual recap') states this as an unqualified absolute, and nothing in §5's Summarise & Review loop or §6B's normalise-and-submit logic carries the refrigerant exception forward. A team building strictly from this document could implement B's gate as always-soft, missing the one legally-relevant block scope requires.
findings.fix: Add one explicit rule to §5B/§6B, and add the carve-out to §12's 'never blocks Save' statement: submission is blocked in exactly one case — refrigerant mentioned in the note but the refrigerant form not completed — matching scope B4 Rule 4 and §7 verbatim. This is deterministic, rule-based logic consistent with the rest of B's non-AI completeness checks, not a new AI capability.

findings.finding: The vector-store seeding decision (Open Item #3) is still open, and the document's own §7B math shows the current sizing assumption is stale by roughly two orders of magnitude: 'one record per completed dispatch' against §12's 200,000+ jobs per six months, versus the superseded 3-4K figure that §4's compute-sizing table and §10's ~$5/month cost line still carry. Index tier, query latency, re-index duration, and the cost line all key off this unresolved number.
findings.fix: Decide between (a) a filtered subset (reason text above the §6C admission threshold and/or a recent-months window) or (b) the full corpus, then re-derive §4's sizing, pin the index type/parameters (HNSW m/ef or the managed-service equivalent), and update §10's vector-store cost line accordingly.

findings.finding: No cascading-deletion mechanism is defined for B's MongoDB collections (summaries, summary_edits) against SQL-side deletion requests (Open Item #10). The document itself flags these as 'original records, not rebuildable' — unlike C's vector index, which is derived from SQL Server and can simply be re-seeded, there is currently no way to honour a request to delete a customer's or job's data from these AI-owned collections.
findings.fix: Define at least an interim mechanism now — e.g., a scheduled or on-demand job that deletes AI MongoDB records by dispatchId when the corresponding SQL Server record is deleted — before this becomes a live customer request with no defined process.

findings.finding: The Dev environment is explicitly permitted to run against Google Gemini (an external third party) specifically because its dataset is 'de-identified/synthetic' rather than a raw production snapshot (Open Item #13) — but the actual de-identification or synthesis technique (which fields are altered, by what method, whether it reuses the production PII scrub or is a separate process) is not specified anywhere in the document, only the requirement that it happen. The entire privacy justification for Dev's Gemini access currently rests on an unbuilt, undescribed control.
findings.fix: Specify the Dev dataset's de-identification/synthesis method in enough detail that it could be audited — e.g., 'reuses the §6B/§12 PII scrub applied to a copy of production data' or 'fully synthetic records generated from X' — before Dev is wired to Gemini.

findings.finding: The entire '~$0 marginal cost' travel-time design for Auto Dispatch — and by extension a meaningful share of the document's cost story — rests on an unconfirmed assumption (Open Item #11, referenced four separate times across §3/§4/§6/§10): that ClimatePros' existing Azuga fleet-telematics contract actually covers the ~28,000 new lookups/day this feature adds. If it doesn't, the real cost is the metered alternative the document itself calculates: ~$4,000-4,200/month, roughly 20x the entire rest of the cloud bill.
findings.fix: Get written confirmation from ClimatePros (or Azuga) that the existing contract's terms and rate structure cover this incremental call volume before relying on the ~$0 figure in any client-facing cost conversation; if it doesn't, budget the metered alternative instead.

findings.finding: The core facts §4's capacity-validation plan needs — the generation model's exact tag/revision, parameter count, quantisation scheme, GPU model/count and VRAM, and measured throughput (max sustained requests/minute) — are all still placeholders pending on-prem hardware access (Open Item #1). The measurement plan and exit gate (a Staging load test before Phase-3 expansion) are well-designed, but as of this document, the system's actual capacity to serve B/C at the target scale is unknown.
findings.fix: Prioritise the private-runtime integration test and hardware-capacity measurement — everything else in §4/§8's admission-control sizing depends on this single number (max-sustained-requests/minute).

findings.finding: The three largest Azure/AI-tier cost lines (Container Apps, vector store, Azure Monitor) still use AWS rate-card estimates rather than real Azure prices (Open Item #2); Cosmos DB is the one real Azure quote, and it too is unverified for the final region/tier. The document is transparent about this via a prominent 'Pending re-pricing' warning box, but the fact remains: the headline ~$179-255/month totals are not yet a number a client could budget against.
findings.fix: Obtain real Azure list pricing for Container Apps, the selected vector-store product, and Azure Monitor, and re-run the cost tables before this is used in any budget conversation.

findings.finding: §6A's tie-break rule uses 'lowest ETA' (free-time-until-free plus travel time) as its first criterion, where scope A2 Rule 5 specifies 'fewer minutes left on the current job' (free-time alone, without travel time). These produce different results whenever two technicians share an equal combined ETA via different free-time/travel-time splits — e.g. Tech A (5 min free, 10 min travel) vs. Tech B (8 min free, 7 min travel) both have eta=15 and would tie under the architecture's rule, but scope's rule picks Tech A (fewer minutes left on the current job).
findings.fix: Change the tie-break's first criterion from 'lowest ETA' to 'fewest minutes left on the current job' (i.e., free_i alone) in §6A's pseudocode and prose, matching scope A2 Rule 5 exactly.

findings.finding: Scope A2 Business Rules 1 and 6 define concrete candidate-eligibility filters — a technician must be a service (not construction/modernisation) technician, not on approved time off, and not already holding one active plus one scheduled non-low-priority job (with emergencies exempt from, but never stacked on top of, this limit). The architecture's Figure 4/§5 describes this only as 'build the candidate list — nearby, eligible technicians, read via the .NET APIs,' without stating whether Auto Dispatch computes this filter itself or consumes it pre-computed from existing platform data, and without restating the workload-limit/emergency-stacking predicate anywhere in §6A.
findings.fix: Add a short paragraph to §5/§6A stating where the eligibility filter (service-vs-construction, time-off, workload limit, emergency-stacking) is evaluated and by what component, and restate the workload-limit predicate explicitly so a reader doesn't need to consult the scope document to know the exact rule.

findings.finding: Scope §9 defines explicit success measures for Auto Dispatch (A) and Parts Finder (C) — for A, the share of dispatches auto-assigned without escalation, the share arriving within the confirmed response window, and the dispatcher override rate; for C, the top-3 hit-rate and the share of sourcing sessions resolved without a return visit. Only B's target ('up to roughly half') is restated in the architecture's §1 Overview; A's measures aren't mentioned there at all, and only one of C's two measures (top-3 hit-rate) appears, in §9 rather than §1.
findings.fix: Add a one-line cross-reference for A's and C's success measures in §1 (even just 'see scope §9') so a reader doesn't need the companion scope document to know what 'success' means for those two use cases.

findings.finding: The MongoDB collections' field-level shapes are given as 'indicative,' with final schema and index design explicitly deferred to a client-DBA sign-off session (Open Item #5). This is reasonable staging, but it means query-performance characteristics for retrieval and the eval dashboard aren't yet confirmed.
findings.fix: No action needed ahead of the DBA session beyond what's already planned; track the sign-off date so it doesn't silently slip past the Phase-1 build start.

findings.finding: The generation model's exact tag/revision, total/active parameter count, and quantisation scheme remain placeholders (Open Item #1/#8) — the mechanism for pinning it (a tag field at the LiteLLM gateway, with a served-tag-divergence alert) is fully specified, but the actual value isn't populated, so the specific model in production use isn't yet knowable from this document.
findings.fix: Populate the model identity fields once on-prem hardware access and integration testing land (same dependency as FND-006).

findings.finding: The document asserts that 'self-hosted model/tooling licences (qwen3-vl-moe, vLLM, bge-m3) are confirmed for commercial deployment' without naming the actual licence type (e.g., Apache 2.0, MIT, a custom model licence) or citing a source anywhere in the document — a reviewer or future engineer can't verify the claim from what's written.
findings.fix: Add a one-line licence citation per self-hosted component (name + licence type + link/reference) rather than an unqualified 'confirmed' assertion.

findings.finding: The model-call contract states a hard request timeout (~10s ceiling over ~6-7s typical) but only says there is 'a max-token ceiling' without giving the actual number — a client implementer can't size buffers or predict worst-case response size from this.
findings.fix: State the actual max-token value for the generation call (and the embedding call, if different) alongside the timeout figures already given.

findings.finding: Every row in §9's 11-signal alert table lists its Owner as 'to assign — techjays on-call / ClimatePros ops' — meaning no alert currently has a specific accountable team or person, only a placeholder naming two possible parties.
findings.fix: Assign a real owner (specific team or on-call rotation) to each alert-table row before go-live; an alert with no accountable owner risks nobody actually responding when it fires.

findings.finding: Whether ClimatePros wants the Google Gemini fallback enabled at all — and if so, under what data-use/DPA terms (region, retention, legal basis) — remains an open decision (Open Item #9). This is correctly a pending decision rather than a live violation: Gemini ships off by default and is technically unreachable while disabled.
findings.fix: Close Open Item #9 with ClimatePros before enabling the Gemini fallback in any environment that could see production-derived data; document the region/retention/legal-basis decision once made.

findings.finding: C's correction-based feedback loop (technician confirms/removes predicted parts → labelled signal, mirroring B's summary_edits) is described only as a 'planned Phase-2 extension.' At launch, C's continuous-improvement loop is thinner than B's, though the pre-launch offline backtest gate provides real protection against a bad model change in the meantime.
findings.fix: Consider whether a minimal version of C's correction-based loop can ship alongside B's rather than deferring wholesale to Phase 2 — the self-reinforcement-avoidance design already built into C's index-admission criteria suggests the harder design problem is already solved.

findings.finding: No per-technician or per-dispatch unit economic (e.g., $/technician/month, $/dispatch, $/closeout) is given anywhere in §10 — only aggregate monthly totals by scenario. This makes it harder to reason about margin or to scale the cost story to a headcount change.
findings.fix: Add one simple unit economic (e.g., total monthly cost ÷ ~900-1,000 technicians, or ÷ ~700 dispatches/day × 30) alongside the existing scenario table.

findings.finding: The AWS→Azure cross-cloud network path is still an open decision between the target state (VPN/VNet peering) and an interim locked-down public HTTPS endpoint with compensating controls (Open Item #6). This is well-mitigated if the interim path is chosen (mTLS, IP allow-list, WAF, rate limits, a dated migration deadline), but the decision itself — and therefore the final security posture and P95 latency budget — isn't yet made.
findings.fix: Decide the pilot posture (VPN/peering vs. interim endpoint) before build starts, per the document's own stated gate, and if the interim path is chosen, assign the migration deadline and owner that are currently placeholders.

findings.finding: The .NET-side mechanism that triggers C's completion push (POST /parts/completions) — a synchronous call on dispatch completion versus an outbox row drained by a scheduled job — and its owning team both remain undecided (Open Item #4). Without this trigger firing reliably, the self-learning index never updates, though a monitor on index-growth rate would at least detect the failure.
findings.fix: Decide the trigger mechanism — the document's own analysis favours the outbox pattern as more robust under AI-tier outages — and assign an owning team.

findings.finding: The Table of Contents' page numbers are increasingly out of sync with the actual document from §4 onward, drifting from roughly +2 pages at §2 to roughly +19 pages by the Appendix — likely because substantial content was added during the v1.2→v1.3 revision without regenerating the TOC. Not a functional problem since the document's own convention is to cross-reference by §N, but a rough edge for anyone navigating by page number.
findings.fix: Regenerate the Table of Contents' page numbers against the final v1.3 pagination before this leaves Draft status.

findings.finding: The crossTierBufferMinutes field's numeric MIN-MAX range is specified as '<to confirm with ClimatePros>' in the OpenAPI reference — the field, type, and default are fully specified, only the bounds are pending.
findings.fix: Confirm the MIN-MAX range with ClimatePros and populate it in the OpenAPI spec.

findings.finding: The role/party responsible for triggering a model-tag change is stated as '<ROLE — to confirm: ClimatePros infrastructure with techjays sign-off>' — the deployment mechanism itself is fully specified, only the accountable role is pending.
findings.fix: Confirm the specific role or team with ClimatePros before go-live.

findings.finding: No representative version numbers are given for the named Python libraries (FastAPI, pydantic, httpx, redis.asyncio, etc.) beyond 'Python 3.11+,' despite the document stating that 'runtime libraries are version-pinned in a lockfile.'
findings.fix: List at least the major/minor version of each named library alongside the lockfile claim, so the stack is verifiable from the document itself.

questions: Does the referenced companion OpenAPI file (Stream1-AI-API.openapi.yaml v1.0.0) exist and match what §8 describes (full request/response schemas, examples, per-endpoint error codes)? It wasn't available alongside the architecture document for this review.

Is the candidate-eligibility filter for Auto Dispatch (service-vs-construction technicians, time-off, the workload limit, emergency-stacking prevention — scope A2 Rules 1 & 6) existing FieldJetX platform logic that Auto Dispatch simply reads via the .NET APIs, or new logic this project must build? The architecture document doesn't say.

Given ClimatePros operates only in the US (46 branches across 50 states, per the scope document), is any specific regulatory regime (e.g., a state privacy law) intended to govern the data-deletion gap in FND-003, or is this purely a matter of ClimatePros' own contractual commitments to its customers? Neither document names a specific regulation.
What is the actual reason-text length/information threshold for C's index-admission criteria (§6C, referenced internally as FND-029)? The mechanism is specified; the number is a placeholder.

Does the Azuga contract's rate structure (fixed-fee vs. per-lookup, and any volume ceiling) actually accommodate a ~28,000-lookups/day increase, or would accommodating this volume require a contract renegotiation even if the relationship in principle 'covers' auto-dispatch?
